name: Mirtazapine

lead: Mirtazapine is a prescription antidepressant approved in the US for major depressive disorder. Its sedating and appetite-increasing effects lead to off-label use for insomnia and appetite loss, which is why people trying to gain weight or sleep better are interested in it.

It is thought to block alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, raising noradrenergic and serotonergic activity, and also blocks several serotonin receptors and histamine H1, which is linked to sedation. Better sleep and easier weight gain are the route toward a fresher face and fuller physique; no trial has tested it for appearance goals.

paras: It is taken on prescription, usually in the evening because of its sedation. People using it for weight or sleep describe the appetite and rest effects as the point, with changes building over weeks.

Reported effects include drowsiness, weight gain, dry mouth, constipation and raised cholesterol. The label has a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts in young people and lists agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome and QT prolongation. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Mirtazapine is sedating and increases appetite, so some people use it off-label for sleep and for gaining weight. Better sleep and easier weight gain lead toward a fresher face and fuller physique. It is approved for depression.

lead: Mirtazapine is a tetracyclic antidepressant, classed as a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant, sold as Remeron. The US label lists major depressive disorder in adults as its indication [1][2].

It is discussed in sleep and recovery contexts because it is sedating and increases appetite; off-label uses reported in reference sources include insomnia, PTSD, anxiety disorders and appetite stimulation in medical illness [1]. No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads about it that could be cited.
The label carries a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviors in young people and lists agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome, angle-closure glaucoma and QT prolongation among warnings [2].

paras: Grokipedia reports FDA approval on 14 June 1996 for major depressive disorder, based on placebo-controlled six-week trials [1]. The label lists only that indication and states it is not approved for pediatric patients [2]. Network meta-analyses comparing antidepressants include mirtazapine among the drugs ranked for efficacy and acceptability [3][4]. A 2011 Cochrane review described in Grokipedia found faster onset than SSRIs at two weeks [1].
Off-label uses described include insomnia, PTSD, panic disorder, OCD, generalized anxiety and appetite stimulation [1].

The label says the mechanism is unclear but may involve antagonism of central presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors and heteroreceptors, enhancing noradrenergic and serotonergic activity [2]. Grokipedia adds blockade of 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, 5-HT3 and histamine H1 receptors, with H1 blockade contributing to sedation [1].

Grokipedia reports drowsiness in up to 54 percent of users, weight gain or increased appetite in 12-17 percent, dry mouth, constipation and raised cholesterol [1]. The label lists suicidality warnings, agranulocytosis, serotonin syndrome, angle-closure glaucoma and QT prolongation [2]. A 2011 cohort study examined antidepressant use and adverse outcomes in older people [5].

Large network meta-analyses compared 21 and 12 antidepressants for acute major depression [3][4]. Registered trials include small studies on mirtazapine in functional dyspepsia, weight gain, sleep disorders in Alzheimer's disease and cancer-related weight loss, and extension trials of its enantiomer esmirtazapine in insomnia [6][7][8][9]. No studies were found testing mirtazapine for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: FDA approves mirtazapine for major depressive disorder [1].
